w00d0.t: Week 0 · Day 0 — Where do you stand?

quiz.q: In the middle of a self-test you meet a question you do not know. What do you do?
options: Run the code or query to check
Write your best guess and mark it with ?
Open the answer key for that one question
quiz.explain: The tests exist to find gaps, so no searching or running anything; a marked guess is fine (→ section 0).

quiz.q: Your SQL self-test score is shown below. Which SQL weeks do you take in full?
quiz.code: SQL 6/8
quiz.explain: 7+ skips weeks 1–3; 5–6 skips week 1 only (→ section 6).

quiz.q: These are your five scores. Which weeks do you skip (checkpoint only)?
quiz.code: SQL 7/8 · Excel 5/8 · Python 8/8 · Statistics 6/8 · BI 5/6
quiz.explain: 7 of 8 skips SQL and Python, 5 of 6 skips BI; Excel 5 and Statistics 6 are below the bar, and week 8 is never skipped (→ section 6).

quiz.q: You skip week 4 because Excel scored 7/8. What must you still do?
options: Take the Excel self-test again on Monday
quiz.explain: Skip means checkpoint only; if you fail it, you take the week after all (→ section 0, rule 4).

quiz.q: Which part of the course is never skipped, whatever your scores?
options: Week 8 (product analytics + capstone) and the Company & metrics track
quiz.explain: Week 8 and the Company & metrics track are the job itself (→ section 6).

quiz.q: BI has only 6 questions. What is the lowest BI score that lets you skip week 7?
quiz.explain: BI: 5 of 6 or better = skip; the other four modules need 7 of 8 (→ section 0, rule 4).

quiz.q: The hand-in box names the file for your plan. What is that file called?
quiz.explain: The plan is my-plan.md, handed in with the 📎 box on this page before Day 1 (→ section 7).

quiz.q: Collections asks which borrowers crossed 30 days late. Which of the two lending questions is that?
options: Are we lending enough, to the right people? (growth)
Neither — it is a marketing question
quiz.explain: Days past due, buckets and write-offs belong to the risk side (→ section 9).

w01d1.t: Week 1 · Day 1 — How a company keeps its data

quiz.q: In the loans table, one row is…
options: one loan that was actually paid out
quiz.explain: Applications are requests; a loan row exists only once money was paid out (→ section 2, The eleven tables).

quiz.q: installments.loan_id appears on many rows. What kind of key is it?
options: Neither — it is just a number
quiz.explain: It repeats, so it cannot be the primary key; it points to loans.loan_id, so it is a foreign key (→ P3).

quiz.q: Which of these are 'what happened' tables?
quiz.explain: Products and branches describe who/what; payments, actions and applications record events (→ P6).

quiz.q: What is the relationship between customers and loans?
quiz.explain: One customer can have many loans; each loan belongs to exactly one customer (→ section 2, One-to-many).

quiz.q: Bekzod asks 'how much are we owed right now?'. Which column is the WRONG one to sum?
quiz.explain: Principal is the original amount lent, not what is still owed (→ P7).

quiz.q: Run this query in any SQL box on this page. How many rows does it count?
quiz.code: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans;
quiz.explain: If you got a different number, you changed your practice copy: Database → ↺ Reset brings the original back (section 1).

quiz.q: One word: all loans currently outstanding, taken together, are called the…
quiz.explain: Company corner: 'the portfolio grew 4 %' means total outstanding went up.

quiz.q: A loan whose status is written_off is…
options: a loss removed from the live portfolio after a very long delinquency
a loan moved to another branch
quiz.explain: Written off = we no longer expect the money; it may still be partly recovered later (→ P9).

quiz.q: What does this query return on the Nur Finance data?
quiz.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers
WHERE monthly_income = NULL;
options: The number of customers with an empty income
quiz.explain: NULL is not a value, so = NULL is never true; empty cells are found with IS NULL (→ section 1, IS NULL — the empty cell).

quiz.q: How does the database read this WHERE clause?
quiz.code:
WHERE product_id = 5 AND status = 'approved'
   OR status = 'approved_not_disbursed'
options: It refuses to run without parentheses
quiz.explain: AND binds tighter than OR, so every approved_not_disbursed application of any product slips in, with no warning (→ section 1, AND, OR, NOT; P11).

quiz.q: Why is this filter wrong for 'applications made in 2025'?
quiz.code: WHERE applied_at BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31'
options: applied_at holds a date and a time, so applications on 31 December after midnight are dropped

quiz.q: Which WHERE clauses return the customers who live in Nukus or Termez?
quiz.explain: IN is a short OR; AND asks for a row that is in both cities at once and returns nothing (→ P7).

quiz.q: 108 rejected applications have an empty credit_score. Where do they appear in this result?
quiz.code:
SELECT application_id, credit_score
FROM applications
WHERE status = 'rejected'
ORDER BY credit_score DESC;
options: They are left out of the result
quiz.explain: Both engines treat NULL as the smallest value, so DESC puts it last and ASC puts it first (→ P10).

quiz.q: You work in SQLite. Which query gives the five biggest loans?
options: SELECT TOP 5 loan_id, principal FROM loans ORDER BY principal DESC;
SELECT loan_id, principal FROM loans ORDER BY principal DESC LIMIT 5;
SELECT loan_id, principal FROM loans ORDER BY principal LIMIT 5;
SELECT loan_id, principal FROM loans LIMIT 5 ORDER BY principal DESC;
quiz.explain: TOP is SQL Server; SQLite puts LIMIT at the very end, and without DESC you get the smallest five (→ section 1, LIMIT and TOP).

quiz.q: A customer was approved but walked away without taking the money (status approved_not_disbursed). For the approval rate, this application counts as…
quiz.explain: Approval is about our decision, not the customer's (→ section 6, Company corner).

quiz.q: Approval rate, convention B (cancelled left out of the denominator): 8 595 approved, 14 000 applications, 1 817 cancelled. Answer in %, one decimal.
quiz.explain: 8 595 / (14 000 − 1 817) = 8 595 / 12 183 ≈ 70.5 %, versus 61.4 % with all applications; always say which convention (→ section 6, Company corner).

w01d3.t: Week 1 · Day 3 — Tables that talk to each other

quiz.q: In a production design, installments.loan_id is a FOREIGN KEY to loans.loan_id. What does it refuse?
options: An instalment whose loan_id does not exist in loans
Many instalments for the same loan
Deleting a loan that still has instalments
A loan with no instalments yet
quiz.explain: The FK keeps the child from pointing at nothing; one-to-many is allowed, and it constrains the child, not the parent (→ section 1, Foreign key).

quiz.q: In Sevara's sheet, the columns inst1_due, inst1_paid, inst2_due, inst2_paid… repeat the same fact across columns. Which normal form does that break?
options: None — it is fine for short loans
quiz.explain: A repeating group breaks 1NF; the fix is one row per instalment, the installments table (→ section 1, 1NF).

quiz.q: In this sheet, rate depends on product, not on the loan. Which normal form is broken, and what goes wrong?
quiz.code:
loan_id | customer | product       | rate | branch_phone
1       | Kamola   | Consumer loan | 0.30 | 71-200-01-01
2       | Kamola   | Consumer loan | 0.30 | 71-200-01-01
options: 3NF — when the Consumer rate changes, thousands of cells must change and some get missed
No form is broken; rate is a number
quiz.explain: A column depending on another non-key column is a 3NF violation and causes update anomalies; the rate belongs in products (→ section 1, 3NF).

quiz.q: What does this statement do?
quiz.code:
UPDATE scratch_restructurings
SET status = 'approved';
options: Approves the most recent row only
Approves every row in the table
quiz.explain: UPDATE and DELETE without WHERE hit every row; write the WHERE first and run it as a SELECT (→ section 1, UPDATE … SET … WHERE).

quiz.q: On SQLite with foreign keys off (PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF, the engine's own default), you run this. Loan 999999 is not in scratch_loan_keys. What happens?
quiz.explain: A constraint protects you only if the engine enforces it; SQLite checks FKs only while PRAGMA foreign_keys is ON (→ P11).

quiz.q: On which tables may you run INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE in this course?
options: Any table, as long as you use WHERE
Only tables whose name starts with scratch_ or my_
quiz.explain: The eleven course tables are read-only, or every expected number on every page stops being true (→ section 1, DDL and DML).

quiz.q: One loan's schedule, as of 2026-10-01. How many days past due (DPD) is the loan?
quiz.code:
installment_no | due_date   | paid
1              | 2026-07-01 | in full
2              | 2026-08-01 | nothing
3              | 2026-09-01 | in full
quiz.explain: DPD counts from the oldest unpaid instalment (1 August), however many later ones were paid: 31 + 30 = 61 days, bucket 61–90 (→ section 5, Company corner).

quiz.q: First-payment default (FPD) jumps at one branch while later buckets stay calm. What is this the classic signal of?
quiz.explain: A borrower who never meant to repay skips the very first instalment; genuine trouble arrives later (→ section 5, Company corner).

w01d4.t: Week 1 · Day 4 — Warehouses, stars and a detective case

quiz.q: Why does the board pack come from the warehouse, not from the production (OLTP) database?
options: Load: a big scan slows the cashiers' screens
History: production overwrites, the warehouse keeps every month-end
Consistency: a report re-run five minutes later should give the same number
The warehouse is always normalised to 3NF
quiz.explain: Load, history and consistency; production can be queried, and the warehouse is de-normalised on purpose (→ section 1, The data warehouse).

quiz.q: One word: the answer to 'what is one row of this fact table?' is called its…
quiz.explain: Choose the grain first; every measure must make sense at it (→ section 1, Grain).

quiz.q: Risk wants 'approval rate by channel, per month'. Which fact table has the right grain?
quiz.explain: Approval is a property of an application, and rejected ones never become loans; write the question, find the noun that is one row (→ section 2).

quiz.q: In a warehouse, dim_branch points to a separate dim_region table instead of storing region itself. What is this design called?
quiz.explain: A snowflake normalises its dimensions: fewer repeated values, one more join in every query; analysts prefer stars (→ section 1, The star schema).

quiz.q: Suppose a duplicate query returned this pair (an invented example). What do you conclude?
quiz.code:
customer_id | name          | birth_date | phone        | region
1111        | Aziz Rakhimov | 1980-05-12 | +99890111... | Samarkand
2222        | Aziz Rakhimov | 1980-05-12 | +99893555... | Andijan
options: A duplicate — same name and birth date
Probably two different people: a match on name and birth date is only a suspicion, and the phones differ
Delete the newer row right away
quiz.explain: Name + birth date + phone is a duplicate; name + birth date alone also catches namesakes sharing a birthday (→ section 3, step 4).

quiz.q: In SQLite, which query finds customers whose first name carries an extra space?
options: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE first_name <> TRIM(first_name);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE first_name = TRIM(first_name);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE first_name = UPPER(first_name);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE first_name IS NULL;
quiz.explain: TRIM returns a copy without the spaces; a row that differs from its own trimmed copy has a space. SQL Server ignores trailing spaces when it compares text, so there compare DATALENGTH instead (→ section 3, step 2).

quiz.q: The data is as of 2026-10-01. Which filter lists the impossible birth dates, including one like 2027-02-28?
quiz.explain: 2027-02-28 is a valid date, so only a business check (born before today, after about 1920) catches it; the BETWEEN version lists the plausible ones (→ section 3, step 5).

quiz.q: "The approval-rate tile shows 61 % and Risk's deck says 70 % — align them." Whose desk does this request come from?
quiz.explain: The BI specialist owns one truth on one screen, including definitions like the two approval-rate conventions (→ section 6, Company corner).

w01d5.t: Week 1 · Day 5 — Checkpoint: design and query

quiz.q: In Nur Pay, one employee can have several advances. Where does the foreign key go?
options: In a column listing all advance ids on the employee row
quiz.explain: The many side holds the key; a list of ids in one cell would also break 1NF (→ Part A, scoring).

quiz.q: An advance can be covered by two payroll runs (the first was short), and one payroll run covers many advances. How do you model that?
options: A repayments table, one row per advance per run, with FKs to both advances and payroll_runs
Store the run dates in a text column on the employee
quiz.explain: Like payments with its two FKs (loan and instalment), a linking table holds one row per pairing (→ Part A; Day 3, section 1, The ER diagram).

quiz.q: Strictly, salary belongs to the employee. When is it right to also store salary_at_request on each advance?
options: When the salary can change later and you must still explain the limit approved at that moment
When the employee has more than one advance
quiz.explain: A snapshot is redundancy chosen on purpose: without it, next month's salary file overwrites the fact the decision was based on (→ Part A; Day 3, P15).

quiz.q: Which WHERE clause returns the same rows as this one?
quiz.code: WHERE NOT (segment = 'mass' OR region = 'Tashkent')
quiz.explain: De Morgan: NOT (a OR b) = NOT a AND NOT b (→ B17).

quiz.q: How many rows of this small table does the query count?
quiz.code:
id | segment  | region
1  | mass     | Tashkent
2  | affluent | Tashkent
3  | mass     | Nukus
4  | sme      | Fergana
5  | affluent | Bukhara

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t
WHERE NOT (segment = 'mass' OR region = 'Tashkent');
quiz.explain: Only rows 4 and 5 are neither mass nor in Tashkent; 4 is the answer you get if you turn the OR into OR NOT (→ B17).

quiz.q: What does this filter count?
quiz.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers
WHERE last_name LIKE '%ova';
quiz.explain: % stands for any characters before; it is a text pattern, not 'female' (surnames in -eva are missed), so say what you measured (→ B8).

quiz.q: The three largest payments are equal amounts on the same loan, paid a month apart. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A duplicate load — delete two of them
Three consecutive instalments of the same size
quiz.explain: Equal monthly amounts are what an annuity schedule produces; check the dates before calling something a duplicate (→ B18).

quiz.q: Which of these mistakes give a wrong number with no error message?
options: Mixing AND and OR without parentheses
Writing = NULL instead of IS NULL
BETWEEN '…-01-01' AND '…-12-31' on a column that also holds a time
quiz.explain: The first three run and quietly return a wrong count; the last two fail loudly, which is the safer kind of mistake (→ Day 2, section 1).

w02d1.t: Week 2 · Day 1 — Joining tables: the loan with its customer

quiz.q: What happens when you run this?
options: One row per loan with the customer id
quiz.explain: customer_id exists in both tables, so the database cannot tell which one you mean; prefix every column (→ section 1, The shape of a join).

quiz.q: customers LEFT JOIN loans returns more rows than customers INNER JOIN loans. Why?
options: LEFT JOIN counts every loan twice
Customers without a loan keep one row each, with NULL in the loan columns
LEFT JOIN also adds loans without a customer
It is a bug in the join condition
quiz.explain: LEFT keeps every row of the left table and fills the right side with NULLs when nothing matches (→ section 1, INNER vs LEFT).

quiz.q: A small bank has 10 customers. 7 of them have loans — 12 loans in total — and 3 have none. How many rows does customers LEFT JOIN loans return?
quiz.explain: 12 loan rows + 3 customers with no loan; check this arithmetic every time you LEFT JOIN (→ section 1, INNER vs LEFT).

quiz.q: What does this query return?
quiz.code:
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM customers c
JOIN loans l ON l.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE l.loan_id IS NULL;
options: The number of customers who never borrowed
0 — the INNER JOIN already removed customers without a loan
The number of loans with no customer
quiz.explain: The anti-join needs LEFT JOIN; an inner join never produces the NULL rows the filter is looking for (→ section 1, the anti-join; P8).

quiz.q: This join returns 92 193 rows. What is one row of the result?
options: One instalment, with its loan's columns repeated
quiz.explain: The grain of a join result is the grain of the many side; SUM(l.principal) here would count each principal once per instalment (→ section 1, Many-to-one).

quiz.q: Starting FROM loans with INNER JOINs, which joins keep the result at one row per loan?
quiz.explain: Many-to-one joins find exactly one partner per loan; one-to-many joins to installments or payments multiply the rows (→ section 1, Many-to-one; P13).

quiz.q: You want loan 1's full schedule with its payments, including instalments not paid yet. Which join?
quiz.explain: The schedule is the left table; an inner join would hide every open instalment (→ P6).

quiz.q: Bekzod asks 'how much principal is still outstanding as of 2026-10-01?'. Which query answers it?
options: SUM(total_due) of matured instalments with no payment
quiz.explain: Outstanding is the principal not yet due on the schedule; SUM(principal) is what was originally lent, and matured-unpaid is the overdue amount (→ section 6, Company corner).

w02d2.t: Week 2 · Day 2 — Counting and summing: the portfolio in numbers

quiz.q: Which line has the bug?
quiz.code:
1  SELECT b.branch_name, COUNT(*) AS loans
2  FROM loans l JOIN branches b ON b.branch_id = l.branch_id
3  WHERE COUNT(*) > 900
4  GROUP BY b.branch_name;
options: Line 3 — a condition on an aggregate belongs in HAVING, after GROUP BY
quiz.explain: WHERE filters rows before grouping, when no count exists yet; HAVING filters groups (→ section 1, WHERE vs HAVING).

quiz.q: What does SQL Server do with this query?
options: Refuses it: loan_id is neither aggregated nor in GROUP BY
Returns one row per product with the first loan_id
quiz.explain: Every SELECT column is either inside an aggregate or in GROUP BY; SQLite silently picks one loan_id, which you must never rely on (→ section 1, GROUP BY one column).

quiz.q: Micro shows 2 669 for COUNT(*) and 2 133 for COUNT(DISTINCT l.customer_id). Which sentence is right?
options: 2 669 Micro loans taken by 2 133 different people
534 Micro loans are duplicates to delete
quiz.explain: COUNT(*) counts rows (loans); COUNT(DISTINCT …) counts different customers — report the one you mean (→ section 1, COUNT).

quiz.q: In SQLite, the method column holds these five values. How many rows does the query return?
quiz.code:
method: 'card', 'card', 'Card', 'cash', 'CASH '

SELECT method, COUNT(*)
FROM payments
GROUP BY method;
quiz.explain: GROUP BY groups exact values: card, Card, cash and 'CASH ' (trailing space) are four different groups (→ P8).

quiz.q: You join loans to payments and want SUM(l.principal). Which quick check tells you the sum is unsafe?
options: The sum is a round number
quiz.explain: If rows outnumber loans, each principal is counted several times; aggregate a column at the grain of its own table (→ section 1, Aggregating over a join; P15).

quiz.q: Which statements about set operators are true?
options: UNION ALL keeps duplicates and is faster
EXCEPT returns rows of the first query that are not in the second
UNION puts two tables side by side, like a join
The two queries must return the same number of rows
quiz.explain: Set operators stack results, so the column count must match, not the row count; default to UNION ALL (→ section 1, Set operators).

quiz.q: Which clause can use a column alias defined in SELECT (e.g. ORDER BY active_loans) on both SQL Server and SQLite?
quiz.explain: ORDER BY runs after SELECT in FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY; SQL Server needs the expression repeated in GROUP BY (→ section 1, The order a query runs in).

quiz.q: In SQLite, what does this column compute per channel?
quiz.code:
SELECT channel,
       ROUND(100.0 * AVG(status LIKE 'approved%'), 1)
FROM applications
GROUP BY channel;
options: The approval rate in %, with all applications as the denominator
The approval rate with cancelled applications left out
The average credit score of approved applications
quiz.explain: A comparison is 1 or 0, so its average is the share that is 1 — here over every application of the channel (→ section 6, Company corner).

w02d3.t: Week 2 · Day 3 — Strings, numbers and dates: cleaning as you query

quiz.q: What does this return, on SQL Server and SQLite alike?
quiz.explain: Two integers divide as integers, so the fraction is cut off; put 100.0 * at the front of every percentage (→ section 1, Integer and decimal division).

quiz.q: And what does this return?
quiz.explain: Still integer division: 791 700 / 14 000 = 56.55, truncated (not rounded) to 56; 100.0 gives 56.55 (→ section 1, Integer and decimal division).

quiz.q: Which filter is right for 'payments received in February 2026'?
quiz.explain: Half-open: start inclusive, next period exclusive — safe for dates, datetimes and any month length; MONTH() = 2 takes every year's February (→ section 1, Filtering a period).

quiz.q: GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(method)) — which raw values end up in the same group?
quiz.explain: Case and end spaces are fixed by LOWER and TRIM; a different word needs REPLACE (→ section 1, UPPER and LOWER to REPLACE).

quiz.q: On SQL Server, this finds no customers although 18 first names end with a space. Why?
quiz.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers
WHERE LEN(first_name) <> LEN(TRIM(first_name));
options: TRIM does not exist on SQL Server
LEN ignores trailing spaces, so both sides are equal; compare DATALENGTH instead
quiz.explain: SQLite's LENGTH counts the space, SQL Server's LEN does not (→ section 1, LENGTH; P4).

quiz.q: How do you find loans that were paid out before the customer applied?
options: WHERE disbursed_at < applied_at on the loans table alone
Join loans to applications on application_id and keep l.disbursed_at < date(a.applied_at)
Join loans to customers and compare with registered_at
Sort loans by disbursed_at and look at the first rows
quiz.explain: applied_at lives in applications, so it is a date comparison across two tables joined on their key (→ section 2, Detective).

quiz.q: Sevara asks for 'average lateness by product'. Which pair of numbers keeps that question honest?
options: Share of payments that are late (how often) and average days of the late payments (how late)
Total late days and number of products
quiz.explain: An average over all payments mixes frequency with severity; report both and name them (→ P18).

quiz.q: In the DPD query, why is the condition HAVING COALESCE(SUM(p.amount), 0) < i.total_due, rather than 'instalments with no payment at all'?
options: A partly paid instalment is still past due; counting only unpaid-at-all ones drops loans from the 90+ bucket
HAVING is required whenever a JOIN is used
quiz.explain: The definition is the oldest instalment not fully paid; token payments would otherwise hide defaulted loans (→ section 6, Company corner).

w02d4.t: Week 2 · Day 4 — NULLs, CASE and the tricky joins

quiz.q: customers has 6 040 rows, 356 of them with no income. Why does this return 5 684 and not 6 039?
quiz.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers
WHERE monthly_income <> 5000000;
options: Nobody earns exactly 5 000 000, so it is a coincidence
A comparison with NULL is unknown, not true, so the 356 rows fail the test too
quiz.explain: NULL rows leave every filter, = and <> alike; when groups do not add up to the total, look for a NULL (→ section 1, Comparing with NULL).

quiz.q: Four customers have these incomes (in millions). What does the query return?
quiz.code:
monthly_income: 10, 20, 30, NULL

SELECT AVG(monthly_income) FROM customers;
quiz.explain: AVG drops the NULL and averages the three known values; it does not treat the unknown as 0 (that would give 15) — report the count next to the average (→ section 1, NULL in aggregates).

quiz.q: Where do customers with an empty income land in this result?
quiz.code:
CASE WHEN monthly_income <  5000000 THEN '<5m'
     WHEN monthly_income < 20000000 THEN '5-20m'
     ELSE '20m+' END AS income_band
options: In '20m+' — every test on NULL is unknown, so they fall through to ELSE
They are left out of the result
In a NULL band of their own
quiz.explain: Put WHEN monthly_income IS NULL THEN 'unknown' first, or the people we know least about join the richest band (→ section 1, Searched CASE).

quiz.q: Which expressions give the NUMBER of approved applications?
options: SUM(CASE WHEN status LIKE 'approved%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
COUNT(CASE WHEN status LIKE 'approved%' THEN 1 END)
COUNT(CASE WHEN status LIKE 'approved%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
AVG(CASE WHEN status LIKE 'approved%' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)
quiz.explain: COUNT counts non-NULL values, so the ELSE 0 version counts every row; the AVG version is the share, not the count (→ section 1, CASE inside SUM and COUNT).

quiz.q: What goes wrong in this LEFT JOIN?
quiz.code:
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM installments i
LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.installment_id = i.installment_id
WHERE p.paid_at <= '2026-10-01';
options: The WHERE test fails on NULL, so every instalment without a payment is dropped: the LEFT JOIN acts as an INNER JOIN
quiz.explain: A filter on the right-hand table belongs in ON (… AND p.paid_at <= '2026-10-01') (→ section 1, The LEFT JOIN that turns into an INNER JOIN; P12).

quiz.q: What is NULLIF for in x / NULLIF(y, 0)?
options: It turns a zero divisor into NULL, so a group with nothing to divide by gives NULL instead of a division-by-zero error
quiz.explain: NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a = b; its one job is safe division (→ section 1, NULLIF).

quiz.q: In this self-join, what does a.customer_id < b.customer_id do?
quiz.code:
FROM customers a JOIN customers b
  ON a.phone = b.phone
 AND a.birth_date = b.birth_date
 AND a.customer_id < b.customer_id
options: Keeps each pair once and never pairs a row with itself
Nothing — it can be left out
quiz.explain: Without it every row matches itself and every pair appears twice, as (a, b) and (b, a) (→ section 1, Joining on two columns).

quiz.q: Why does the FPD30 base include only loans whose first instalment fell due at least 30 days before the as-of date?
options: Younger loans have not had their 30 days yet, so they would count as 'not FPD' and make young vintages look perfect
Because newer loans have no instalments
quiz.explain: Every loan in the base must have had the chance to fail; forgetting the scope is the classic FPD trap (→ section 6, Company corner).

w02d5.t: Week 2 · Day 5 — Checkpoint: 25 questions from four teams

quiz.q: Bekzod asks for outstanding principal by product. What is one row of the table you aggregate?
quiz.explain: Outstanding is the sum of principal_due on instalments with due_date after the as-of date; loans and products are joined only as labels (→ T2, T25).

quiz.q: Madina asks for disbursements by month. Which join, made before SUM(l.principal), silently inflates the number?
quiz.explain: products, branches and dim_date are many-to-one from the loan; installments repeats each loan once per instalment (→ T25).

quiz.q: Two loans: loan 1 has principal 100 and 3 instalments, loan 2 has principal 200 and 2 instalments. What does the query return?
quiz.explain: Each principal is counted once per instalment: 100 × 3 + 200 × 2 = 700, not 300; COUNT(*) vs COUNT(DISTINCT l.loan_id) (5 vs 2) would have warned you (→ interview question 8).

quiz.q: The data runs to 2026-10-01 and Q3 must end on 30 September. Which line has the bug?
quiz.code:
1  SUM(CASE WHEN l.disbursed_at >= '2026-01-01' AND l.disbursed_at < '2026-04-01' THEN l.principal ELSE 0 END) AS q1,
2  SUM(CASE WHEN l.disbursed_at >= '2026-04-01' AND l.disbursed_at < '2026-07-01' THEN l.principal ELSE 0 END) AS q2,
3  SUM(CASE WHEN l.disbursed_at >= '2026-07-01' THEN l.principal ELSE 0 END) AS q3
options: Line 3 — it has no upper bound, so 1 October leaks into Q3
quiz.explain: Every period needs a half-open range with both ends: >= start AND < next start (→ T7).

quiz.q: Sevara wants delinquent loans that have NEVER had a collections action. Which shape is right (dpd = the delinquent loans)?
options: FROM dpd d LEFT JOIN collections_actions ca ON ca.loan_id = d.loan_id WHERE ca.action_id IS NULL
FROM dpd d JOIN collections_actions ca ON ca.loan_id = d.loan_id WHERE ca.action_id IS NULL
FROM dpd d LEFT JOIN collections_actions ca ON ca.loan_id = d.loan_id WHERE ca.outcome IS NOT NULL
FROM collections_actions ca LEFT JOIN dpd d ON d.loan_id = ca.loan_id WHERE d.loan_id IS NULL
quiz.explain: The anti-join: the population you count goes on the left, and IS NULL on the right key keeps the unmatched ones; the inner version always returns 0 (→ T13).

quiz.q: Is this filter safe for the 31–90 call list?
quiz.code: WHERE d.dpd BETWEEN 31 AND 90
options: Yes — dpd is a whole number and BETWEEN includes both ends
quiz.explain: The BETWEEN trap is on dates that carry a time; on integers it is exact (→ T10).

quiz.q: Which habits belong to the working method of weeks 1–2?
options: Write the noun that is 'one row' before aggregating
Run COUNT(*) next to COUNT(DISTINCT key) after a one-to-many join, before summing
Filter periods half-open (>= start, < next start)
Put the NULL test first in a CASE
Use BETWEEN with the month's last day for monthly reports
Leave the count out next to a rate to keep slides clean
quiz.explain: BETWEEN with an end date drops times on the last day, and a rate without its count hides how small the base is (→ Working method, top of the page).

quiz.q: A monthly FPD30 vintage has about 300 loans and 3 FPDs, so one loan moves the rate by 0.3 points. How do you read it?
options: Compare single months and report every jump
Read vintages by quarter (or longer) and show the counts next to the rates
Drop the months with zero FPDs
quiz.explain: Small counts make monthly rates noisy; group them and always show the base (→ T18; Day 4, Company corner).

w03d1.t: Week 3 · Day 1 — Window functions: a total next to every row

quiz.q: In this query, what does the outer SUM(…) OVER () add up?
quiz.code:
SELECT p.code, SUM(i.principal_due) AS outstanding,
       100.0 * SUM(i.principal_due) / SUM(SUM(i.principal_due)) OVER () AS share_pct
FROM installments i JOIN loans l ON l.loan_id = i.loan_id
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = l.product_id
WHERE i.due_date > '2026-10-01'
GROUP BY p.code;
options: Every instalment of the company again, row by row
The five per-product sums, giving the grand total on each of the five rows
It is an error — aggregates cannot be nested
quiz.explain: The inner SUM is the GROUP BY aggregate; the window runs on the grouped result and adds those values up (→ section 1, Share of total — value / SUM() OVER ()).

quiz.q: What does total show on each row?
quiz.code:
SELECT loan_id, principal,
       SUM(principal) OVER () AS total
FROM loans
WHERE customer_id = 3208;
options: The total principal of customer 3208's loans only
The principal of the row itself
quiz.explain: Windows are computed after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, so the window only sees the rows that survived the filter (→ section 1, OVER (); P1).

quiz.q: Why does this fail, and where does the window go instead?
options: Windows do not exist yet when WHERE runs; compute the window in a derived table or CTE and filter outside
Put the window in GROUP BY instead
It does not fail — it returns loans above their product's average
quiz.explain: Wrap, then filter (→ section 1, Where a window may appear; P13).

quiz.q: Three rows, ordered as shown. What is run on the FIRST row (the default frame, RANGE)?
quiz.code:
day        | x
2026-09-28 | 10
2026-09-28 | 20
2026-09-29 | 5

SELECT day, x, SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS run FROM t;
quiz.explain: RANGE takes every row with the same ORDER BY value, so both 28 September rows show the day's total, 30; ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING would give 10 (→ section 1, The frame — ROWS BETWEEN; P11).

quiz.q: Bekzod wants a year-to-date running sum per product. What is wrong with this?
options: Without PARTITION BY code the running sum runs across all products, so Auto's YTD includes every other product too
ORDER BY is not allowed inside OVER
quiz.explain: PARTITION BY restarts the running sum per group (→ section 1, ORDER BY inside OVER; P5).

quiz.q: Which window gives a 3-month moving average of monthly disbursement (this month and the two before)?
options: AVG(disbursed) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
AVG(disbursed) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
AVG(disbursed) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING)
quiz.explain: 2 PRECEDING + the current row = 3 months; 3 PRECEDING is four months, the 1/1 frame is a centred average, and no frame is a running average (→ section 1, Moving average; P12).

quiz.q: Which of these need a window function (GROUP BY alone cannot do it)?
options: Every loan with its product's average principal beside it
Each product's outstanding with its share of the total in the same row
One total of outstanding per product
Monthly disbursement with a running year-to-date column
The number of loans in the company
quiz.explain: Windows keep rows and add a group's number, a total or a running sum beside them; plain totals are GROUP BY (→ section 1, Window vs GROUP BY; P6).

quiz.q: By loan count the book is mostly Consumer, Micro and BNPL; by money it is mostly SME and Auto. What should a portfolio-mix table show?
options: Money share only — it is what the board cares about
Count share and money share side by side, saying share of what
quiz.explain: Count speaks to operations, money to risk; a share without 'of what' is meaningless (→ section 6, Company corner).

w03d2.t: Week 3 · Day 2 — Ranking and looking sideways: ROW_NUMBER, LAG and the duplicate payments

quiz.q: Three loans share the top principal; a fourth is next. What do ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK (ORDER BY principal DESC) give the fourth loan?
quiz.explain: ROW_NUMBER never repeats; RANK gives ties one number and then skips; DENSE_RANK gives ties one number with no gap (→ section 1, RANK and DENSE_RANK).

quiz.q: You need exactly one row per customer: their latest loan. Which function, and which filter?
options: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY disbursed_at DESC, loan_id DESC), keep rn = 1 in an outer query
quiz.explain: ROW_NUMBER guarantees one row even on ties, the tiebreaker makes it repeatable, and the filter goes outside because windows do not exist in WHERE (→ section 1, Top-N per group; P9).

quiz.q: NTILE(4) over these 10 rows: how many rows land in group 1?
quiz.code:
SELECT x, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY x) AS g
FROM t;      -- t has the 10 values 1, 2, …, 10
quiz.explain: NTILE cuts into groups of almost equal count; the leftover rows go to the first groups: 3, 3, 2, 2 (→ section 1, NTILE; P4).

quiz.q: Why does last_payment show each row's own date?
options: With ORDER BY, the default frame ends at the current row, so the 'last' row of the frame is the row itself
quiz.explain: Spell out ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, or use FIRST_VALUE with ORDER BY … DESC (→ section 1, FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE).

quiz.q: m holds monthly disbursement and the query computes yoy_pct with LAG(disbursed, 12). Someone moves the display filter WHERE month >= '2026-01' inside m. What happens?
quiz.code:
WITH m AS (SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', disbursed_at) AS month, SUM(principal) AS disbursed
           FROM loans
           WHERE disbursed_at >= '2026-01-01' AND disbursed_at < '2026-10-01'
           GROUP BY 1)
SELECT month, disbursed, LAG(disbursed, 12) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS same_month_last_year
FROM m;
options: 2025 is gone before the window runs, so every year-on-year value is NULL
LAG reads 2025 from the loans table anyway
quiz.explain: Filter the display in an outer query; the window can only look back at rows that reached it (→ section 1, LAG and LEAD; P5).

quiz.q: To clean duplicate payments you number rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY installment_id, paid_at, amount ORDER BY payment_id). Why not just GROUP BY … HAVING COUNT(*) > 1?
options: HAVING finds the duplicate groups but cannot say which row to keep or return the clean rows alongside; the window does both
GROUP BY cannot take three columns
quiz.explain: Keep rn = 1 (the earliest payment_id) as a view; never DELETE from the raw table (→ section 1, Duplicates; section 2, step 2).

quiz.q: You build a DPD snapshot as of 2026-09-01 from data extracted on 2026-10-01. Where must the as-of date appear?
options: In the payment join: p.paid_at <= '2026-09-01' (in ON)
quiz.explain: A payment made on 15 September must not count on 1 September, and in a LEFT JOIN the payment condition belongs in ON (→ section 1, Roll rates with LAG; section 5).

quiz.q: To build the roll-rate matrix you join the September and October DPD snapshots with a FULL OUTER JOIN. Why not an INNER JOIN?
options: INNER JOIN is not allowed between CTEs
A loan that cured is only in September and a newly late loan only in October; an inner join drops both
quiz.explain: Neither side may lose rows; absent = DPD 0 with COALESCE (→ section 5, Company corner).

w03d3.t: Week 3 · Day 3 — Subqueries, CTEs and the vintage curve

quiz.q: closed_at is NULL for every loan still open. What does this return, and why?
quiz.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans
WHERE disbursed_at NOT IN (SELECT closed_at FROM loans);
options: The loans disbursed on a day no loan was closed
0 — one NULL in the list makes NOT IN unknown for every row
quiz.explain: x <> NULL is unknown; add WHERE closed_at IS NOT NULL inside, or use NOT EXISTS (→ section 1, IN with a subquery; P3).

quiz.q: Which statements about NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM loans l WHERE l.customer_id = c.customer_id) are true?
options: It stops at the first matching row
It cannot multiply rows, even for a customer with seven loans
A NULL in the inner table simply never matches, so there is no NULL trap
It needs an IS NULL test on a right-hand column
It can show the matching loan's columns in the output
quiz.explain: IS NULL on a carefully picked column and right-side columns in the output belong to the LEFT JOIN anti-join (→ section 1, EXISTS and NOT EXISTS).

quiz.q: What does this query return?
quiz.code:
SELECT loans_per_customer, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS loans_per_customer
      FROM loans GROUP BY customer_id) AS t
GROUP BY loans_per_customer;
options: One row per customer with their loan count
How many customers have 1 loan, 2 loans, 3 loans …
An error — GROUP BY cannot be used twice
quiz.explain: A derived table lets you aggregate twice: first per customer, then per count (→ section 1, Derived table; P4).

quiz.q: What makes a subquery correlated?
options: It returns more than one row
It refers to a column of the outer query's current row, so conceptually it runs once per outer row
It sits in the FROM clause
quiz.explain: E.g. WHERE l.principal > (SELECT AVG(x.principal) FROM loans x WHERE x.product_id = l.product_id) (→ section 1, Correlated subquery; P5).

quiz.q: How many rows does this calendar have?
quiz.code:
WITH RECURSIVE months(month_start) AS (
  SELECT '2026-01-01'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(month_start, '+1 month') FROM months
  WHERE month_start < '2026-06-01')
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM months;
quiz.explain: The anchor gives January; each step adds a month while the last one is before June, so June is the last row: January to June (→ section 1, Recursive CTE; P8).

quiz.q: When does a CTE chain beat nested subqueries?
options: When the same result is needed twice, when nesting goes deeper than two levels, or when someone must read the steps top-down
When you need a single scalar value
quiz.explain: A chain fixes one grain per step and reads like a recipe; a one-line scalar or a single EXISTS is fine as a subquery (→ section 1, CTE; A chain of CTEs).

quiz.q: A loan's late30 flags for instalments 1–6 are 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0. What does MAX(late30) OVER (PARTITION BY loan_id ORDER BY installment_no) give?
quiz.explain: The running MAX turns a per-instalment event into 'ever late so far', which stays on once set (→ section 1, The vintage table).

quiz.q: At MOB 3 the 2026-03 cohort shows 3.98 % ever-30+, and the 2025-03 cohort shows 9.94 % at MOB 6. Is the new book cleaner?
options: Not from these two cells: compare cohorts at the same MOB (read down a column)
No — newer cohorts are always worse
quiz.explain: The newer cohort is younger, not necessarily better; at MOB 3, 2025-03 was 5.59 % (→ section 5, Company corner).

w03d4.t: Week 3 · Day 4 — Views, temp tables and making it fast

quiz.q: You have v_loan_status (a view) and t_loan_status (CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT * FROM v_loan_status). A payment is added tonight. Which is true tomorrow?
options: The view shows it, the table does not — but the table is faster to read
The table shows it, the view does not
Neither shows it until you re-create both
quiz.explain: A view stores the query text and recomputes on every read; a materialised table stores a frozen result (→ section 1, What a view is; When a view, when a table).

quiz.q: due_date has an index. What does the plan say for this filter, and how do you fix it?
options: SEARCH — the index is used; nothing to fix
SCAN — the function hides the column; write due_date >= '2026-09-01' AND due_date < '2026-10-01'
An error — functions are not allowed with indexes
quiz.explain: The engine cannot look up a value it must compute per row; the half-open range turns the scan into a SEARCH (→ section 1, Reading EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN; habit 3; P11).

quiz.q: ix_payments_method indexes method, and other columns have their own indexes. In which filters can an index NOT help?
options: WHERE is_weekend = 1 (a column with two values)
JOIN payments p ON p.installment_id = i.installment_id
quiz.explain: A function on the column, a leading %, and a two-value column defeat the index; equality, ranges and joins on the indexed column benefit (→ section 1, Indexes — the phone book).

quiz.q: In SQL Server, what is a clustered index?
options: Any index on two or more columns
The table itself, stored in the index's order — so there is only one per table
A copy of the table on another server
An index that only works with GROUP BY
quiz.explain: Non-clustered indexes are separate sorted structures pointing into the table; you can have many (→ section 1, Indexes — the phone book).

quiz.q: A report summed principal over loans JOIN installments and came out 24× too big. Someone 'fixes' it like this. What is still wrong?
options: With an instalment column in the list every row is still distinct, so nothing collapses; fix the grain by aggregating instalments per loan first, then join
DISTINCT cannot be used with JOIN
quiz.explain: DISTINCT hides a join bug only by accident, and is slow; aggregate at each grain, then join (→ section 1, The habits that make queries fast, habit 4; P12).

quiz.q: You have just created v_loan_status (one row per loan). Which check do you run first?
options: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT loan_id) FROM v_loan_status — the two must be equal
quiz.explain: The grain check: if rows exceed distinct loans, a join multiplied; every view ships with its check query (→ section 2, Worked example; section 6).

quiz.q: A tiny book of four loans as of today. What is PAR30 in %?
quiz.code:
loan | dpd | outstanding
A    |   0 | 100
B    |  15 |  50
C    |  45 |  30
D    | 120 |  20
quiz.explain: PAR30 = outstanding of loans with DPD > 30 ÷ total outstanding = (30 + 20) / 200 = 25 %; NPL90 would be 20 / 200 = 10 % (→ section 6, Company corner).

quiz.q: PAR30 is 3.12 % and NPL90 is 2.55 %. What do two such close numbers tell you?
options: The data is wrong — they should be far apart
Most of the money at risk is already 90+: the delinquent book is mostly old debt
Collections is doing an excellent job
quiz.explain: PAR30 includes NPL90; when they are close, little sits in 31–90 and most at-risk outstanding is past 90 days (→ section 6, Reading the six together).

w03d5.t: Week 3 · Day 5 — Checkpoint: the loan-book EDA report

quiz.q: Which of these cost the number point in the report?
options: Summing loans.principal after a join to installments
LAG with the display filter inside the CTE, so year-on-year comes out NULL
Printing 0.00 % in a vintage cell that is not yet observable
quiz.explain: The last two are the required habits, not mistakes (→ Common mistakes from this week).

quiz.q: In S2, what does SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER () add up in the SECOND block?
quiz.code:
SELECT 'product' AS dim, p.code AS value, COUNT(*) AS loans,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1) AS share_pct
FROM loans l JOIN products p ON p.product_id = l.product_id GROUP BY p.code
UNION ALL
SELECT 'grade', risk_grade, COUNT(*),
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1)
FROM loans GROUP BY risk_grade;
options: The grade groups of its own block only, so each block adds to 100
Every row of both blocks, so the shares add to 100 across the whole result
Nothing — windows are not allowed with UNION ALL
quiz.explain: Each SELECT of a UNION ALL is computed on its own before stacking; check that each block adds to 100 (→ S2).

quiz.q: Why does every payment sum in the report read v_payments_clean with paid_at <= '2026-10-01'?
options: To drop the exact duplicate payments and the payments dated after the as-of date
Because raw payments has no amount column
quiz.explain: Raw payments carries repeats and forward-dated rows; the clean view plus the as-of filter gives the figure you can defend (→ S3, S4).

quiz.q: Monthly disbursement in a toy series. What is mom_pct for March?
quiz.code:
month   | disbursed
2026-01 | 100
2026-02 |  80
2026-03 | 120

ROUND(100.0 * (disbursed - LAG(disbursed) OVER (ORDER BY month))
      / LAG(disbursed) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS mom_pct
quiz.explain: (120 − 80) / 80 = +50 %; a month-on-month swing like this is why the trend is read on a moving average (→ S7).

quiz.q: A vintage cell is not yet observable: only some of the cohort's loans have had their 30 days at that MOB. What goes in the cell?
quiz.explain: A zero would say 'nobody late' when nobody was measured (→ S9; Day 3, Company corner).

quiz.q: Month-end outstanding for 30 September is a little lower than the as-of outstanding on 1 October. Which explanation is right?
options: One of the two queries is wrong
Month-end leaves out loans disbursed on 1 October and still counts instalments due on 1 October; two correct numbers, two definitions
quiz.explain: Write both definitions in the dictionary and reconcile them, rather than forcing one to match the other (→ S8; Day 4, P8).

quiz.q: Duplicate rows turn up in a production payments table. What is the safe way to handle them?
options: DELETE the second rows right away
Define sameness, list the rows with ROW_NUMBER, show the owner the rows and the money, check downstream effects, publish a de-duplicated view, propose a unique constraint at load
Copy the table to Excel and remove duplicates there
quiz.explain: The raw table stays as evidence; reporting reads the clean view (→ Part B, question 8).

quiz.q: Which sentence is a finding rather than a description of the table?
options: The table has five rows, one per product.
By count this is a Micro/Consumer/BNPL lender; by money it is an SME/Auto lender.
The query groups loans by product code.
SME is one of the five products.
quiz.explain: A finding is something Bekzod could read aloud and act on, with share of what and period stated (→ Working method).

w04d1.t: Week 4 · Day 1 — Excel for analysts: the sheet is a table

quiz.q: You type this in B3 and fill it right to F3 and down to row 10. What does $A3 do?
quiz.code: =SUMIFS(tblLoans[outstanding], tblLoans[region], $A3, tblLoans[bucket], B$2)
options: Keeps column A fixed while the row moves, so every cell reads its region from column A
Keeps row 3 fixed while the column moves
Pins the single cell A3 for every copy
quiz.explain: $ before the letter pins the column, before the number pins the row; B$2 does the opposite for the bucket labels (→ section 1, Relative and absolute references; Worked example).

quiz.q: Which criterion counts both approved and approved_not_disbursed applications?
quiz.explain: * is any characters, like LIKE 'approved%'; "approved" alone is Marketing's lower rate, and <>rejected also lets cancelled in (→ section 1, Wildcards in criteria; section 6).

quiz.q: The method column of a small table holds these five values. What does the formula return?
quiz.code:
method: card | Card | CARD | 'card ' (trailing space) | cash

=COUNTIFS(tblPayments[method], "card")
quiz.explain: Excel criteria ignore case, so card, Card and CARD all match; a trailing space is still a different value (→ section 1, COUNTIFS, SUMIFS, AVERAGEIFS; P8).

quiz.q: What does an Excel Table (Ctrl+T) give your formulas that a plain range like K2:K7829 does not?
options: Structured references such as tblLoans[outstanding] that mean the whole column
Auto-expansion: new rows pasted under the table are included
Calculated columns: one formula fills every row
quiz.explain: Excel stays case-insensitive and has no NULL, Table or not (→ section 1, Excel Tables).

quiz.q: B2 may hold the bucket label as the number 0, while tblLoans[bucket] holds the text "0". Which formula is a reliable test that B2 is the wrong type?
options: =ISTEXT(B2) — FALSE means B2 is a number, not the text "0"
=COUNTIFS(tblLoans[bucket], B2) — a non-zero result proves B2 is text
quiz.explain: ISTEXT / ISNUMBER test the type, and = or SUMPRODUCT(--(a<>b)) compare strictly; COUNTIFS and SUMIFS may treat number-like text as numbers, so they are not a safe test. Type the label as '0 (→ section 2, Worked example; Mistakes that cost a point).

quiz.q: A1 = 1 and A2 = 4. A cell holds =100*A1/A2 and is formatted 0.0%. What does it show?
quiz.explain: The % format already multiplies by 100; write =A1/A2 and let the format do it (→ section 1, Number formats vs values; Mistakes that cost a point).

quiz.q: You want to count surnames written entirely in lower case. Why does =SUMPRODUCT(--(tblCustomers[last_name]=LOWER(tblCustomers[last_name]))) fail?
options: = ignores case in Excel, so every surname equals its lower-case copy; use EXACT
LOWER does not exist in Excel
quiz.explain: EXACT is the one case-sensitive comparison in Excel (→ section 1, TRIM, UPPER, LOWER, PROPER; P11).

quiz.q: Your Approval sheet has three channel rows. How do you fill the total row's approval rate?
options: The average of the three channel rates
Sum the approved counts and the application counts, then divide once
The highest of the three rates
Type the company figure from last week's SQL
quiz.explain: Averaging rates ignores that channels differ in size (mix); sum the counts, divide once (→ section 6, Company corner).

w04d2.t: Week 4 · Day 2 — Lookups and dynamic arrays: joining in Excel

quiz.q: Lookup!A3:A7 lists the products in product_id order, not alphabetically. What can this return?
quiz.code: =VLOOKUP("Micro loan", Lookup!$A$3:$F$7, 3)
options: Always Micro's rate — the key is exact
Another product's rate or #N/A, with no warning
quiz.explain: Without FALSE, VLOOKUP does an approximate match that assumes a sorted first column; always write FALSE (or 0) for keys (→ section 1, VLOOKUP and its four traps; P3).

quiz.q: Which VLOOKUP traps does XLOOKUP remove?
options: The column number is a count that breaks when a column is inserted
It can only return values to the right of the key
A relative range walks when the formula is copied down
quiz.explain: XLOOKUP is exact by default and takes a return column anywhere; you still pin ranges with $ or use a Table (→ section 1, XLOOKUP — exact match).

quiz.q: The bucket table has lower edges 0, 1, 31, 61, 91 with labels 0, 1-30, 31-60, 61-90, 90+. Which label does this return for dpd = 45?
quiz.code: =XLOOKUP(45, Lookup!$A$11:$A$15, Lookup!$B$11:$B$15, , -1)
quiz.explain: Match mode −1 takes the largest lower edge ≤ 45, which is 31 (→ section 1, XLOOKUP for bands; P6).

quiz.q: Your band table is keyed on the UPPER edges (0, 30, 60, 90, 9999). Which match mode puts dpd 31 in 31-60?
quiz.explain: Upper edges need the next larger edge; −1 on upper edges drops every dpd of 31 into 1-30 (→ Mistakes that cost a point; P6).

quiz.q: You select A2:M7829 and add a formula rule to colour 90+ rows red. Which formula is right?
quiz.explain: $ on the column, not on the row: every cell of a row looks at that row's bucket; $M$2 colours every row by row 2 (→ section 1, Conditional formatting).

quiz.q: =ROWS(UNIQUE(tblLoans[customer])) returns 747, but the book has 4 335 borrowers. Why?
options: customer is a name, not an id: many borrowers share a name
quiz.explain: Keys are ids; a lookup or distinct count on a name column is never a people count (→ section 1, UNIQUE; P10).

quiz.q: When is IFERROR around a lookup the right choice?
options: Always — it keeps the sheet clean
When a miss is expected, the replacement is meaningful, and a check cell counts the misses
quiz.explain: IFERROR(…, 0) under a SUM turns misses into zeros and the total looks complete (→ section 1, IFERROR).

quiz.q: Risk moves to 1–7 / 8–30 buckets. Why does the bucket rule live in a sorted table on Lookup, read by an approximate XLOOKUP, rather than in an IFS formula?
options: You add a row to the table and every formula, colour and count follows — no formula to edit
XLOOKUP is faster than IFS on 7 828 rows
IFS does not work in Google Sheets
quiz.explain: Definition and data stay separate: change a boundary in one cell, never in a formula (→ section 6, Company corner).

w04d3.t: Week 4 · Day 3 — Cleaning dirty data: Find & Replace to Power Query

quiz.q: You tick first_name, last_name, birth_date on the raw Customers sheet and run Remove Duplicates. Why does it miss some true duplicates?
options: It only checks the first 1 000 rows
It ignores case but not spaces, so 'Bobur ' and 'Bobur' stay different rows
It is case-sensitive, so MALIKA and Malika stay apart
It removes the first copy instead of the second
quiz.explain: Remove Duplicates compares exactly as displayed, case-insensitively and space-sensitively; TRIM before matching (→ section 1, Remove Duplicates — and why it lies; P8).

quiz.q: Why does the matching key put a separator between the parts?
quiz.code: =LOWER(TRIM(B2))&"|"&LOWER(TRIM(C2))&"|"&TEXT(E2,"yyyy-mm-dd")
options: Excel needs it to join text
Without it, different names can glue into the same key: 'Ali'&'Nazarov' = 'Alin'&'azarov'
quiz.explain: A separator keeps the parts apart, so only true matches share a key (→ section 1, A matching key).

quiz.q: In N2, filled down the sheet, what does this formula return?
quiz.code: =COUNTIFS($L$2:L2, L2)          (column L holds the key)
options: How many rows in the whole sheet share the key
1 for the first occurrence of a key, 2 for the second, … — Excel's ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key)
TRUE when the key is unique
quiz.explain: The range grows row by row ($L$2 pinned, L2 free), so it counts how many times the key has appeared so far; filter rank = 2 to look at the extras before deleting (→ section 1, COUNTIFS on the key).

quiz.q: On Payments you tick ALL columns in Remove Duplicates 'to be safe'. Why is nothing removed?
options: payment_id differs on every row, so no two rows are equal on all columns; sameness must be defined on installment_id, paid_at and amount
Remove Duplicates does not work on numbers
The table must be sorted first
quiz.explain: A duplicate is two rows that agree on everything that matters, not on everything (→ section 1, Remove Duplicates — the recorded step; Mistakes that cost a point).

quiz.q: Which Power Query steps are matched with the right SQL idea?
options: Merge Queries, join kind Left Outer = LEFT JOIN
Merge Queries, join kind Left Anti = rows with no match (anti-join)
Append Queries removes duplicate rows, like UNION
quiz.explain: Append keeps every row and matches columns by name; Changed Type is CAST (→ section 1, Merge Queries, Append Queries; P14).

quiz.q: A customer was born on 2000-10-02. What age does the formula give as of 2026-10-01?
quiz.explain: "y" counts completed years; the 26th birthday is one day after the as-of date (→ section 2, step 3; P6).

quiz.q: A customer's birth date is 2031-04-12. What goes into customers_clean?
options: The birth date left blank, with birth_date_invalid = TRUE
quiz.explain: Blank + flag, never a guess: an invented date would flow into age bands as if it were real (→ section 2, step 3; P9).

quiz.q: The collection rate for instalments due in September (as of 1 October) is lower than for June–August. Why is that expected?
options: September is always a bad month
September's instalments have had at most 30 days to be paid, the earlier months much longer; the latest month reads low until it matures
Duplicates were removed only for September
The cash-basis rate was used for September
quiz.explain: Compare months at the same age, or wait a month (→ section 6, Company corner; P16).

w04d4.t: Week 4 · Day 4 — Pivot tables and charts: the one-page report

quiz.q: A pivot has region then branch in Rows, and Sum of outstanding shown as % of Parent Row Total. What does a branch row show?
options: The branch's share of the whole book
The branch's share of its own region
The difference from the previous branch
quiz.explain: % of Parent Row Total is SUM(x) / SUM(SUM(x)) OVER (PARTITION BY region); on the region rows it shows the share of the grand total (→ section 1, Show Values As — % of Parent; P3).

quiz.q: You add this calculated field to get the average ticket per product. What do you get?
quiz.code: avg_ticket = principal / loan_id
options: The sum of principal divided by the sum of the loan ids — nonsense, with no error
quiz.explain: Calculated fields work on sums, never counts; use Average of principal in Values, or a column of 1s (→ section 1, A calculated field; P7).

quiz.q: Which chart for disbursements by month over 34 months?
options: A pie, one slice per month
A line, with a 3-month moving average for the trend
A stacked bar sorted by amount
quiz.explain: Time on the x-axis is a line's job; the moving average is the trend, the monthly line the noise (→ section 1, Which chart for which question; section 6).

quiz.q: Which chart rules are not matters of taste?
options: Bars and columns start at zero
Use a pie whenever you show shares
Give every bar its own colour
quiz.explain: A pie hides small slices, and one colour plus one highlight keeps the eye on the point (→ section 1, Chart trap: the pie with many slices; Building an honest chart).

quiz.q: Two branches have 150 and 160 bn outstanding. The column chart's axis starts at 140 bn. How many times taller does the 160 bar LOOK than the 150 bar?
quiz.code: bar heights drawn: 160 − 140 and 150 − 140
quiz.explain: 20 vs 10 units: the eye reads 'twice as big' for a 7 % difference — bars start at zero (→ section 1, Chart trap: the truncated axis; section 2, step 9).

quiz.q: Power Query refreshed this morning with new loans, but the pivot still shows last week's totals. Why?
options: The pivot reads its own cache; it updates only on Refresh (or Refresh All)
The slicer is hiding the new rows
Pivots ignore rows added after creation
quiz.explain: Build on a Table or query output and refresh the pivot after the data (→ section 1, Refresh, the pivot cache and formats that survive it; P10).

quiz.q: A pivot is filtered to the Top 5 branches. You divide its Grand Total by itself to get 'share of the book'. What is wrong?
options: A filtered pivot's Grand Total is the total of the shown rows only, so the share comes out 100 %; divide by the Table's SUM instead
Top-N filters do not change totals
quiz.explain: The denominator must come from the unfiltered book (→ P4).

quiz.q: On 1 October the Disbursements MTD tile shows 21 loans, 0.85 bn. What belongs on the tile?
options: Those numbers labelled as one day, with the last full month (September) beside them
Replace them with September's numbers silently
Hide the tile until the month ends
quiz.explain: A partial period must be marked, never compared with full months without a note (→ section 6, Company corner).

w04d5.t: Week 4 · Day 5 — Checkpoint: cleaned dataset + one-page report

quiz.q: After Refresh All, customers_clean still contains ids above 6 000. What went wrong?
options: No Sort on registered_at before Remove Duplicates, so the later copy was kept instead of the original
The ids were typed as text
quiz.explain: Remove Duplicates keeps the first row it meets; sort so the row you want to keep comes first (→ A1, model answer; If you are stuck).

quiz.q: Three customers' monthly_income (in millions). One blank was typed as 0 during cleaning. What does AVERAGE now return?
quiz.code:
monthly_income: 10 | 20 | 0   (the 0 was a blank)

=AVERAGE(customers_clean[monthly_income])
quiz.explain: With the blank kept as null, AVERAGE skips it and returns 15; a zero income is a statement, a blank is a gap (→ A1, checks).

quiz.q: 24 payments are dated after 2026-10-01. What does payments_clean do with them?
options: Keeps them, flags them with is_forward_dated, and excludes them from as-of sums
Moves them to a separate file
quiz.explain: They are real payments recorded with a future date: nothing destroyed, flagged, filtered where an as-of matters (→ A2).

quiz.q: The reviewer duplicates the last line of payments_dirty.csv and presses Refresh All. What must payments_clean show?
options: The same row count as before — the new line is one more copy of a known payment
quiz.explain: The cleaning is a property of the query, not of the file; a count that changes means something was pasted (→ What the reviewer runs).

quiz.q: Which choices keep the one-pager refreshable?
options: Data arrives through Power Query or a Table
Pivots are built on the Table or query output
Tiles read the pivots with GETPIVOTDATA or the Table with SUMIFS
Number formats are set in Value Field Settings
Pivots built on a fixed range A1:M7829
Tiles pasted as values before sending
quiz.explain: A fixed range never grows and a pasted value never updates (→ Part C, question 8; Common mistakes).

quiz.q: XLOOKUP returns #N/A for a product that is clearly in the Lookup table. What is the likely cause?
quiz.code:
A2 shows: Micro loan
=LEN(A2)  → 11
options: XLOOKUP needs FALSE as the last argument
A trailing space in the key — 'Micro loan' has 10 characters; TRIM it
The Lookup table is not sorted
The product is in a hidden row
quiz.explain: #N/A means nothing matched: check spaces with LEN and numbers stored as text with ISNUMBER (→ Follow-ups a panel asks).

quiz.q: Finance says September's collection rate is 96 %; your tile says 94.1 %. What do you answer?
options: One of the two is a formula error
Different bases: cash basis (all money received in September ÷ due) vs instalment basis (paid on September's instalments ÷ due); both right, name the basis
quiz.explain: Write the basis under the tile and the argument ends (→ Follow-ups a panel asks; Day 3, Company corner).

quiz.q: Which sentence belongs in findings.md?
options: PAR30 is 3.12 % and NPL90 2.55 %, so most at-risk money is already past 90 days: old debt, not a new wave.
I used a pivot table on tblLoans.
quiz.explain: Each finding carries a number and a consequence the board can act on (→ Part B, findings note).

w05d1.t: Week 5 · Day 1 — Python from zero: the notebook is your lab

quiz.q: You change the function in cell 3, then re-run only cell 7, which calls it. Which version does cell 7 use?
options: Whichever cell is higher on the page
The new one — Jupyter re-reads every cell above
The old one — the kernel remembers what was last run, not what is on the screen
quiz.explain: The kernel keeps variables in the order cells were run; Kernel → Restart & Run All is the only proof that a notebook works top to bottom (→ section 1, 'Where your code runs').

quiz.q: What does this print?
quiz.code:
principal = "31150000"      # as read by csv.DictReader
print(principal * 2)
quiz.explain: Every value from a CSV is text, and a string times 2 is the string repeated — convert with int() before any arithmetic (→ P1).

quiz.q: With label() from section 1, what does the last line print?
quiz.code:
def label(dpd):
    if dpd <= 0: return "0"
    elif dpd <= 30: return "1-30"
    elif dpd <= 60: return "31-60"
    elif dpd <= 90: return "61-90"
    else: return "90+"

print(label(30), label(91))
quiz.explain: dpd <= 30 is still 1-30, and 91 is past 90 — the right-closed buckets of week 2 (→ P6).

quiz.q: This loop gives approval rates a few points below week 4's 58.2 / 63.7 / 61.9 %. Why?
options: total.get(ch, 0) resets the count on every row
The rows were not converted with int()
quiz.explain: Status has two 'approved' spellings; startswith("approved") is week 4's "approved*" wildcard — == alone loses 678 approvals (→ section 2).

quiz.q: Approved / applications: app 2 915 / 5 006, branch 3 965 / 6 223, partner 1 715 / 2 771. What is the total approval rate, in %, one decimal?
quiz.explain: Sum the counts: 8 595 / 14 000 = 61.4 %. Averaging the three channel rates gives 61.3 % — never average rates for a total row (→ section 2).

quiz.q: Which statements about rows read with csv.DictReader are true?
options: Numeric columns are converted to int automatically
A blank cell arrives as an empty string ""
Each row is a dict keyed by the header line
sum() skips blank credit scores by itself
quiz.explain: DictReader gives text keyed by the header; convert on use and test for "" first — 388 credit scores are blank (→ section 1, 'Reading a CSV').

quiz.q: A cell fails with a long traceback. What do you read first?
options: Nothing — re-run the cell until it works
The last line (the error type and message), then the arrow at your own code
quiz.explain: The newest call is at the bottom: the last line names the error, the arrow shows the line of your code (→ section 1, 'Errors').

quiz.q: Company corner: loan 1 (24-month annuity) is one year into its term. Its outstanding is…
options: the sum of the 12 remaining payments, interest included
more than 50 %, because the early payments are mostly interest
less than 50 %, because interest is paid off first
quiz.explain: Interest = balance × r is front-loaded, so the principal parts start small; outstanding = principal not yet due — 57 % for loan 1 (→ Company corner).

w05d2.t: Week 5 · Day 2 — pandas I: the DataFrame is a table you can talk to

quiz.q: The loan with index label 0 has dpd = 0. What does the second line do?
quiz.code:
late = loans[loans["dpd"] > 0]
late.loc[0]
options: Raises KeyError — label 0 is not in late
quiz.explain: loc selects by label, iloc by position; after a filter they differ — late.iloc[0] is 'the first late loan' (→ section 1, 'loc and iloc').

quiz.q: This line raises an error. What is the fix?
quiz.code: loans[loans["dpd"] > 0 & loans["status"] == "active"]
quiz.explain: & binds tighter than > and ==, so every condition needs its own brackets; and / or do not work on a whole Series (→ section 1, 'Selecting rows').

quiz.q: What happens to the 7 429 loans with dpd = 0?
quiz.code: pd.cut(loans["dpd"], bins=[0, 30, 60, 90, np.inf])
options: They become NaN — intervals are right-closed, and (0, 30] does not contain 0
pd.cut creates a '0' bucket for them
quiz.explain: The first edge must be below the smallest value (-1 for DPD); np.inf closes the top (→ section 1, 'pd.cut').

quiz.q: On loans_status.csv, what does this give, in % with two decimals?
quiz.code: 100 * loans.loc[loans["dpd"] > 30, "outstanding"].sum() / loans["outstanding"].sum()
quiz.explain: Outstanding of loans with dpd > 30 ÷ total outstanding = 6.51 bn of 208.7 bn = PAR30 (→ Company corner).

quiz.q: Which statements about missing values in pandas are true?
options: fillna(0) on monthly_income gives a lower, wrong mean
mean() skips NaN, like SQL's AVG
dropna() without subset= drops a row if any column is missing
col == np.nan finds the missing rows
count() counts every row, NaN included
quiz.explain: NaN is pandas' NULL: aggregates skip it, == never finds it (use isna()), and fillna(0) on an income is a decision that invents zero earners (→ section 1, 'Missing values').

quiz.q: You count September applications on applied_at, which holds a date and a time. Which filter is right?
quiz.explain: between is inclusive and "2026-09-30" means midnight, so the 30th's afternoon is lost; dt.month == 9 also catches September 2025. Half-open, always (→ section 1, 'Selecting rows', P5).

quiz.q: portfolio_summary counts 3 030 loans disbursed in 2026; week 4's tile said 3 051. Why?
options: parse_dates shifts every date by a day
The function uses < AS_OF, so the 21 loans disbursed on 1 October itself are out
pandas drops rows with NaN dates
quiz.explain: Half-open < AS_OF excludes the as-of day; neither convention is wrong, but the docstring must say which (→ section 2).

quiz.q: Company corner: what is the numerator of PAR30?
options: The whole outstanding of loans with dpd > 30
The number of loans with dpd > 30
The outstanding of loans in the 31-60 bucket only
The overdue instalments of loans more than 30 days late
quiz.explain: A 500 m loan one day past 30 puts the full 500 m into PAR30; overdue ÷ outstanding is the arrears ratio and the count share is another number (→ Company corner).

w05d3.t: Week 5 · Day 3 — pandas II: groupby, merge and the cleaning pipeline

quiz.q: You need each payment's share of its loan's total, on every payment row. Which call gives the loan total per row?
quiz.explain: agg returns one row per group; transform returns one value per original row — the window function SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY) (→ section 1, 'transform').

quiz.q: You expected len(m) == 92 193. Why is it smaller?
quiz.code:
m = inst.merge(paid, on="installment_id")
len(inst), len(m)
options: merge defaults to how="inner", so instalments with no payment vanish
installment_id is text in one of the tables
merge drops rows with NaN in any column
quiz.explain: The default join is inner; use how="left", fillna(0) after the merge, and assert len(m) == len(inst) (→ section 1, 'merge', P6).

quiz.q: inst has 10 instalments; paid has one row for each of the 6 instalments that received a payment. How many rows does m have?
quiz.code:
m = inst.merge(paid, on="installment_id")
len(m)
quiz.explain: The default join is inner: only instalments with a payment survive, and the 4 without a payment — exactly the ones DPD needs — vanish; how="left" keeps all 10 (→ section 1, 'merge').

quiz.q: installments.merge(payments_raw, on="installment_id", validate="1:1") raises MergeError on the raw payments file. What does it tell you?
options: pandas cannot validate more than 50 000 rows
The merge must be rewritten as a loop
Some instalments have more than one payment row (here the duplicate payments), so payments to instalments is m:1 — the grain you stated was wrong
quiz.explain: validate turns a wrong belief about the grain into an error before any number is wrong — the week-2 fan-out, caught (→ section 1, 'validate= and indicator=', P8).

quiz.q: Which statements about duplicated / drop_duplicates are true?
options: Without subset= it compares all columns, and finds 0 payment duplicates because payment_id differs
drop_duplicates keeps the first row in the current order, so sort first
duplicated(keep=False) marks every member of a duplicate group
It always keeps the row with the lowest id, whatever the order
quiz.explain: The key defines sameness, the sort defines the survivor, the assert proves both (→ section 1, 'Duplicates').

quiz.q: pd.to_datetime(birth_date, errors="coerce") produces 0 NaT. Are the birth dates clean?
options: Yes, if the dtype is datetime64
No — parsing is syntax; 2031-04-12 parses fine and still breaks the business rule
No — coerce silently turns bad dates into 1900-01-01
quiz.explain: Validity is a rule you write (not in the future, not before 1920); flag and blank with .where, never guess a date (→ section 1, 'Dates that lie').

quiz.q: What does the concat produce?
quiz.code:
a = pay[pay["region"] == "Tashkent"]
b = pay[pay["region"] != "Tashkent"].rename(columns={"amount": "Amount"})
pd.concat([a, b])
options: All rows and one column more: amount is NaN in b's rows, Amount is NaN in a's
An error: the column names differ
Only the columns both frames share
One amount column — pandas ignores case
quiz.explain: concat matches columns by name, without an error; assert set(a.columns) == set(b.columns) before every concat (→ section 1, 'concat', P9).

quiz.q: Company corner: in the DPD function, a late loan's DPD is…
options: as-of − the due date of its oldest matured instalment that is not fully paid
as-of − the due date of its most recent unpaid instalment
quiz.explain: Per loan: AS_OF − min(due_date) over instalments that are matured and not fully paid; 0 when nothing is late (→ Company corner).

w05d4.t: Week 5 · Day 4 — Charts and the SQL bridge: matplotlib, seaborn, read_sql

quiz.q: Why does the figure pack use fig, ax = plt.subplots() instead of plt.plot()?
options: Every title, label and formatter then belongs to a named chart — clear and safe when there are several
Only a fig can be saved to PNG
quiz.explain: plt.plot draws on 'the current axes', which gets confusing with several charts; the object interface makes the chart yours (→ section 1, 'Figure and axes').

quiz.q: Each bar is meant to be the product's total outstanding. What does it show?
quiz.code: sns.barplot(data=loans, x="outstanding", y="product")
options: The mean outstanding per loan of each product
quiz.explain: seaborn's barplot aggregates with the mean by default — pass estimator=sum or aggregate first (→ section 1, 'seaborn').

quiz.q: sns.heatmap of a vintage matrix (cohort × MOB) needs which shape of data?
options: Wide: a pivot with cohorts as rows and MOB as columns
Long: one row per cohort × MOB
quiz.explain: hue-based charts want long data (melt); heatmap wants a wide matrix (pivot) — most 'seaborn does not work' moments are the wrong shape (→ section 1, 'seaborn').

quiz.q: Both lines return the same count today. Which one belongs in the figure pack?
quiz.code:
as_of = "2026-10-01"
q1 = pd.read_sql(f"SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM payments WHERE paid_at > '{as_of}'", con)
q2 = pd.read_sql("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM payments WHERE paid_at > ?", con, params=(as_of,))
options: Neither — read the whole table and filter in pandas
q2 — params= passes the value safely; an f-string breaks on a quote and invites injection on a real server
quiz.explain: Values go in params=, never into the SQL text (→ section 1, 'read_sql', P11).

quiz.q: On nur.db, what number does this query return?
quiz.code: pd.read_sql("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM payments WHERE paid_at > ?", con, params=("2026-10-01",))
quiz.explain: 24 forward-dated payments (53.4 m) — the rows every payment sum excludes with paid_at <= AS_OF (→ section 1, 'read_sql').

quiz.q: Which of these are chart rules, not matters of taste?
options: No legend for a single series
A log axis on a bar chart so small values show
A second y-axis so two lines fit
Drop the one-day October point from a time series
quiz.explain: A log axis breaks 'bars from zero', and two y-axes invent crossings; the October point (one day) reads as a crash (→ section 1, 'What chart for what question').

quiz.q: Figure 2's title says "208.7 bn". Next month the total changes. What is the lasting fix?
options: Add a footnote with the date
Build the title from the data with an f-string
Edit the title by hand each month
quiz.explain: A title computed from the data cannot go stale; an assert above the chart catches a changed extract (→ section 2).

quiz.q: Company corner: what makes the figure pack Timur's and not a favour?
options: One AS_OF used in every query, titles computed from the data, an assert before each chart — then Restart & Run All
quiz.explain: Reproducibility is the deliverable: change AS_OF, run all, five new files (→ Company corner).

w05d5.t: Week 5 · Day 5 — Checkpoint: the EDA report, in pandas

quiz.q: Every yoy_pct value comes out NaN. Why?
quiz.code:
m26 = m.loc["2026-01":]
m26["yoy_pct"] = m26["disbursed"].pct_change(12) * 100
options: The frame was cut to 2026 before pct_change(12), so no row is 12 months back
quiz.explain: Compute on the full 33-month frame and filter for display afterwards — week 3's LAG trap in a new spelling (→ S7).

quiz.q: Where are the loans whose customer has no income?
quiz.code:
lc["band"] = pd.cut(lc["monthly_income"], [0, 5e6, 10e6, 20e6, np.inf], right=False)
pd.crosstab(lc["band"], lc["risk_grade"])
options: pd.cut raises an error on NaN
Nowhere — the NaN band is dropped from the crosstab silently
quiz.explain: Turn the NaN band into a row (astype(str).replace("nan", "unknown")) — the week-2 NULL-band lesson (→ S10).

quiz.q: Why right=False in the income cut?
options: It keeps NaN as a band
So that [5m, 10m) matches SQL's WHEN monthly_income < 10000000 — a customer earning exactly 5 000 000 stays in the same band as in week 3
quiz.explain: pd.cut is right-closed by default; the SQL rule was '<', so right=False reproduces it (→ S10).

quiz.q: Summing principal after merging instalments onto loans gives ×24.7. Which merge argument would have stopped it?
options: validate= with the grain you expect (e.g. "m:1")
quiz.explain: validate raises MergeError when a key is not unique where you promised — the week-2 fan-out becomes an error (→ 'Common mistakes').

quiz.q: You forgot parse_dates=, yet L["disbursed_at"].max() still returns a value. What is wrong?
options: It is a string comparison that works on ISO text by luck; .dt and date arithmetic are unavailable
quiz.explain: parse_dates= is where the typing happens; without it .max() compares text and still 'works' (→ S3).

quiz.q: Which belong in every checkpoint section?
options: The week-3 number next to yours — an assert where it must be exact, a printed pair where rounding may differ
One finding Bekzod can read aloud
A match / mismatch line that says why
quiz.explain: Three cells per section, not thirty: the reviewer reads the finding, checks the match line, then the output (→ 'Working method').

quiz.q: Which Jupyter command proves the notebook is reproducible before you submit? (Kernel → …)
quiz.explain: Restart & Run All runs every cell from a clean kernel; then save, so the outputs are inside the file (→ 'Rules').

quiz.q: Your pandas number differs from week 3 and the line under it explains why (half-open vs inclusive filter). What does it cost?
options: Nothing — only an unexplained mismatch costs the number points
quiz.explain: A mismatch is not a failure if the line under it says why (→ 'Working method').

w06d1.t: Week 6 · Day 1 — Probability and distributions: how random is a default?

quiz.q: 45.1 % of all FPDs came through the app. What is the FPD rate of an app loan?
quiz.explain: P(app | FPD) answers 'where do defaults come from'; P(FPD | app) answers 'how risky is an app loan' (→ section 1, 'Conditional probability').

quiz.q: What does the second line return?
quiz.code:
X = stats.binom(400, 91 / 7099)
X.sf(10)
